name: Plantar heel pain (plantar fasciopathy)
populations: runners and other physically active adults
people with a higher body mass index
people who stand or walk for long periods
adults with limited ankle dorsiflexion or first MTP extension
summary: A load-related degenerative condition of the plantar fascia at the medial calcaneal tubercle. It causes first-step heel pain that eases with warming up and is managed with education, load control and strengthening.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Often slow: in one hospital cohort 54% were asymptomatic at a mean of 9.7 years, and 50% still had the condition at 5 years

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based and gradual (no validated criteria): pain-controlled loaded single-leg calf work first, then a graded walk–run program

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: First-step pain plus focal tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle. Weight-bearing windlass test: sensitivity 31.8%, specificity 100% in one small study

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to diagnose. Ultrasound shows a thickened fascia (about 6.7–6.9 mm at baseline in one cohort), but thickness did not predict prognosis

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Estimated to affect 7–10% of the population

keyFacts.label: Key treatment
keyFacts.value: High-load heel raises beat plantar-specific stretching at 3 months (Foot Function Index 29 points lower), but groups were equal by 6 and 12 months

overview:
Plantar heel pain, also called plantar fasciopathy or plantar fasciitis, is pain under the heel at or just in front of the medial calcaneal tubercle, where the plantar fascia attaches. The classic feature is sharp pain with the first steps after rest, especially first thing in the morning, which eases with walking and returns with prolonged loading. It is thought to affect 7–10% of the population [r1]. Clinical practice guidelines for physiotherapists exist for nonarthritic heel pain and have been revised several times [r2,r3].

The name 'fasciitis' is misleading. Histology from 50 heel-spur operations for chronic disease showed myxoid degeneration, fragmentation and bone-marrow vascular ectasia, which led the authors to describe a degenerative fasciosis without inflammation [r4]. The working model is a failure to adapt to load: the fascia is repeatedly tensioned during walking and running, partly through the windlass mechanism, and load at its calcaneal enthesis exceeds capacity [r5]. Treatment is education, load management and progressive strengthening, with taping, orthoses, shockwave or injection as adjuncts whose evidence is limited and often conflicting [r6]. In one RCT, high-load heel raises gave better outcomes than stretching at 3 months [r7]. Recovery is often slow, and many people are still symptomatic after a year [r1].

epidemiology.text: Plantar fasciitis is reported to affect 7–10% of the population [r1]. Most evidence on risk factors is cross-sectional, so cause and effect are uncertain. In a meta-analysis of studies of physically active people, those with plantar fasciitis had a greater plantarflexion range of motion (mean difference 7.04°), a higher body mass index (2.13 kg/m²) and a higher body mass (4.52 kg) than those without it; the authors graded the evidence as level 3 [r8]. An earlier review of chronic plantar heel pain found that body mass index in non-athletic people and the presence of a calcaneal spur were the factors most clearly associated with pain. It found some evidence for increasing age, reduced ankle dorsiflexion, reduced first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) extension and prolonged standing. Evidence on foot posture and foot motion was inconclusive, and height, weight and BMI in athletic populations were not associated with heel pain [r9]. The two reviews therefore disagree on BMI in active people and on the direction of the ankle range-of-motion finding.

intrinsic: Higher body mass index and body mass in active individuals (mean differences 2.13 kg/m² and 4.52 kg); an earlier review found BMI associated only in non-athletic people (modifiable) [r8,r9]
Differences in ankle motion: greater plantarflexion range in active people [r8]; reduced ankle dorsiflexion and reduced first MTP extension showed some association in an earlier review [r9]
Calcaneal spur: associated with heel pain, although it did not predict prognosis in a long-term cohort [r9,r1]
Smaller foot-muscle volume and weaker toe and ankle muscles, with very low certainty and unclear direction of cause [r10]
Negative psychological factors (kinesiophobia, pain catastrophising) are associated with worse foot function and first-step pain, but the evidence is cross-sectional [r11]
extrinsic: Running and other repetitive weight-bearing activity in physically active people [r8]
Sudden increases in running, standing or walking volume, hard surfaces or unsupportive footwear (modifiable; clinical observation, not established as risk factors in the reviews cited)

mechanism.summary: Plantar heel pain has no single injury moment. It develops from thousands of loaded steps a day that repeatedly tension the plantar fascia. The fascia is stretched as the arch lowers in early stance, then tightened by the windlass mechanism as the heel lifts and the great toe extends at the first MTP joint, so tensile load is transmitted to its calcaneal enthesis [r5]. When load rises faster than the fascia's capacity to adapt, the tissue at the origin changes structure and becomes painful [r4,r1].
sequence: At heel strike the heel fat pad cushions the impact, and ground-reaction force rises rapidly.
In early stance the foot pronates and the medial arch lowers, so the plantar fascia lengthens and takes tensile load.
In late stance the heel lifts under calf (gastrocnemius–soleus) contraction while the forefoot stays on the ground.

The great toe extends at the first MTP joint and winds the fascia around the metatarsal head (the windlass mechanism). The fascia tightens, the arch rises and the foot becomes a stiff lever for push-off [r5].
Peak tensile load passes into the calcaneal enthesis at the medial calcaneal tubercle, step after step.
When volume or intensity rises faster than capacity, the fascia at its origin degenerates and thickens instead of adapting [r4,r1].
The tissue becomes sensitised. After rest the fascia stiffens, so the first weight-bearing steps load a thickened, painful origin and produce first-step pain that eases as the foot warms up.

variants.name: High-volume running or walking load
variants.description: Running and other weight-bearing sport raise the number and size of tensile cycles per day. Active people with plantar fasciitis had higher BMI and body mass than active people without it [r8].

variants.name: Occupational and standing load
variants.description: Prolonged standing showed some association with chronic plantar heel pain, and BMI was associated in non-athletic people [r9].

variants.name: Restricted ankle or first MTP motion
variants.description: Reduced ankle dorsiflexion and reduced first MTP extension showed some association with heel pain. Both limit how smoothly the windlass can work, but the direction of cause is unproven [r9,r5].

variants.name: Heel spur (traction spur)
variants.description: A calcaneal spur is associated with chronic heel pain but it is not the pain source by itself, and baseline spur did not affect long-term outcome [r9,r1].

variants.name: Coexisting nerve or fat-pad pain
variants.description: The inferior calcaneal (Baxter's) nerve and the heel fat pad lie next to the origin and can contribute to, or mimic, plantar heel pain. A US-guided corticosteroid injection did not cause fat-pad atrophy in one cohort [r1].

anatomy.text: The plantar fascia is a thick fibrous aponeurosis that runs from the medial calcaneal tubercle to the forefoot, where it divides into slips that attach around the metatarsophalangeal joints. Its central band is the part most often involved. It supports the medial longitudinal arch and acts as a tie-rod in the windlass mechanism: extension of the great toe winds the fascia around the first metatarsal head, tightens it and raises the arch [r5]. The heel fat pad cushions the calcaneus. The intrinsic foot muscles (abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis) arise close to the fascial origin, and the inferior calcaneal (Baxter's) nerve runs deep to abductor hallucis near the medial calcaneal tubercle. The Achilles tendon inserts at the back of the same bone, and calf tightness changes how load reaches the foot.

structures.name: Plantar fascia
structures.role: Tension band that supports the medial arch, resists arch flattening and tightens through the windlass mechanism at push-off [r5]

structures.name: Medial calcaneal tubercle (enthesis)
structures.role: Bony origin of the central fascial band; the usual site of tenderness and pathology

structures.name: Heel fat pad
structures.role: Shock-absorbing cushion under the calcaneus at heel strike

structures.name: First MTP joint
structures.role: Great-toe extension drives the windlass mechanism that tightens the fascia

structures.name: Abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis
structures.role: Intrinsic foot muscles that arise near the fascial origin and help support the arch

structures.name: Inferior calcaneal (Baxter's) nerve
structures.role: Mixed nerve that runs near the medial calcaneal tubercle. It is a differential or coexisting source of heel pain.

structures.name: Gastrocnemius–soleus and Achilles tendon
structures.role: Generate push-off force and influence the load passing through the foot (kinetic chain)

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Plantar fasciopathy is best understood as a failure to adapt to repeated tensile load at the fascial origin, not a primary inflammatory condition. In 50 heel-spur operations for chronic plantar fasciitis, histology showed myxoid degeneration with fragmentation and degeneration of the plantar fascia, plus bone-marrow vascular ectasia. The authors argued for 'fasciosis' rather than 'fasciitis' and questioned serial corticosteroid injection, in view of the absence of inflammation and the potential for plantar fascial rupture [r4]. These specimens came from patients with chronic disease who were having surgery, so they say little about the first weeks, and inflammation in early disease cannot be excluded.

Structure and symptoms are only loosely related. In a hospital cohort with ultrasound-confirmed plantar fasciitis, the fascia was 6.7–6.9 mm thick at baseline and fell to 4.3 mm at follow-up in both symptomatic and asymptomatic patients. Baseline thickness and heel spur did not predict prognosis, and only 24% of asymptomatic patients had a normal fascia on ultrasound at long-term follow-up [r1]. Symptoms therefore settle well before imaging normalises, and imaging should not drive treatment decisions.

structures.name: Plantar fascia (proximal, medial band)
structures.effect: Thickening, myxoid degeneration and fragmentation at the origin. Thickness was about 6.7–6.9 mm at baseline in a cohort [r4,r1].

structures.name: Calcaneal enthesis and bone
structures.effect: Bone-marrow vascular ectasia in surgical specimens [r4]. A traction spur is associated with pain but did not predict long-term outcome [r9,r1].

structures.name: Heel fat pad
structures.effect: Normally a cushion. Fat-pad thickness was similar in patients who had a US-guided corticosteroid injection (9.0 mm) and those who did not (9.4 mm), so no atrophy was shown in that cohort [r1].

structures.name: Inferior calcaneal (Baxter's) nerve
structures.effect: Can be irritated or compressed next to the origin and coexist with fasciopathy. Screen for burning, radiating or night pain.

structures.name: Intrinsic foot muscles
structures.effect: Smaller foot-muscle volume and reduced toe plantar-flexion strength were reported in people with heel pain, with very low certainty and inconsistent findings [r10].

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius–soleus
muscles.effect: Calf muscle endurance did not differ between people with and without plantar heel pain (SMD 0.01) [r10]. Higher ankle plantar-flexor strength was one of the strongest predictors of improvement over the medium term in a small prognostic review [r12].

muscles.name: Intrinsic foot muscles and toe flexors
muscles.effect: Hallux and lesser-toe plantar-flexion strength were reduced and foot muscle volume was generally smaller in people with heel pain, but the quality of evidence was very low and the direction of cause is unclear [r10].

muscles.name: Ankle invertors, evertors and dorsiflexors
muscles.effect: Ankle dorsiflexion, inversion and eversion strength were lower in people with heel pain in some studies, with inconsistency between studies [r10].

cellular.timing: Days to weeks of excess load
cellular.description: Repeated tensile load beyond capacity damages collagen at the enthesis. This is the working mechanistic model; early human tissue is rarely sampled, so it is not directly observed.
Myxoid degeneration, fragmentation and loss of orderly collagen, with little inflammatory infiltrate in chronic surgical specimens [r4].
The fascia thickens at its origin. Mean thickness was about 6.7–6.9 mm at baseline in a hospital cohort [r1].

Symptoms settle with load management and progressive loading well before structure normalises: at long-term follow-up only 24% of asymptomatic patients had a normal fascia on ultrasound [r1]. Cellular adaptation to strength training in the plantar fascia has not been directly shown.

systems.effect: First-step pain and sensitivity to load suggest a sensitised enthesis. Pain catastrophising was associated with first-step pain in people with plantar heel pain [r11]. A role for central sensitisation in persistent cases is plausible but not established.
Ankle dorsiflexion, first MTP extension, calf capacity and foot-muscle strength all influence how load reaches the fascia, although the direction of cause is unproven [r9,r10].
Higher body mass and BMI were associated with plantar fasciitis in active individuals, which increases the load per step [r8].

Emotional distress, kinesiophobia and catastrophising are associated with poorer foot function in plantar heel pain [r11]. Psychosocial predictors of outcome have not been tested in prognostic cohorts [r12].

Bilateral heel pain predicted a poorer outcome in two prognostic sources [r1,r12]. Consider an enthesitis-related inflammatory arthropathy when heel pain is bilateral, has morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes or comes with other joint or skin features.

timeframes.summary: There is no fixed healing timeline: the course follows load history and capacity, so the phases below are illustrative and overlap. Symptoms often last many months, and many people are still symptomatic at 1 year [r1].

healing.description: Tensile load exceeds capacity at the origin; first-step pain starts and is often load-related at this stage

healing.phase: Degeneration and thickening if overload continues
healing.description: Myxoid degeneration and thickening of the proximal fascia; pain can become persistent [r4,r1]
Pain and function improve with loading, and the groups in the RCT were equal by 6 months [r7]. Structure may remain abnormal for years [r1].
In a hospital cohort the risk of still having plantar fasciitis was 50.0% at 5 years [r1]

milestones.label: Short-term relief from taping
milestones.note: Taping was an effective short-term treatment in a review of mechanical treatments, with follow-up from 3–5 days [r13]

milestones.label: Strength training ahead of stretching
milestones.note: Foot Function Index 29 points lower (95% CI 6–52) at 3 months with high-load strength training [r7]

milestones.label: Groups equal
milestones.note: No between-group difference at 6 months, and none at 12 months [r7]

milestones.label: One year
milestones.note: FFI was 22 points (strength) and 16 points (stretch) at 12 months; 80.5% still had plantar fasciitis at 1 year in the hospital cohort [r7,r1]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based; no validated criteria exist. Most active people can keep walking and cross-training on a modified load while they rebuild capacity. A return to running is graded over weeks to months once loaded calf work and first-step pain are controlled (clinical convention).

symptoms: Sharp or stabbing pain under the medial heel with the first steps after rest (first thing in the morning or after sitting)
Pain eases with walking and warming up, then returns with prolonged standing, walking or running
Gradual onset over weeks, often after a rise in running, standing or walking volume or a change of footwear
Pain climbing stairs or on tiptoe, and when walking barefoot on hard floors
Often unilateral; bilateral heel pain is less common and should prompt a systemic screen
signs: Focal tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle and the proximal medial band of the fascia
Pain on passive extension of the great toe (windlass) or on a weight-bearing single-leg heel raise in some patients
Reduced ankle dorsiflexion or reduced first MTP extension in some patients
Pes planus or pes cavus in some, but foot posture was not consistently associated with heel pain [r9]
Mild plantar heel thickening or swelling is uncommon; marked swelling, bruising or a pop suggests another diagnosis

subjective: Pain site (plantar-medial heel) and first-step pain: how long it lasts, and whether it eases with walking
Load history: recent change in running, standing or walking volume, surface, footwear or job
Duration and previous treatment, including injections and orthoses
Bilateral symptoms and morning stiffness, other joint pain, psoriasis, bowel or eye symptoms (inflammatory screen) [r1,r12]
Numbness, burning, radiating or night pain (nerve involvement) and any recent trauma
Body mass, diabetes and other comorbidities [r8,r9]
Fear of loading, catastrophising and expectations (psychosocial screen) [r11]
observation: Foot posture (standing and walking): pes planus or cavus, hindfoot alignment
Gait: heel strike, push-off and toe-off, and whether the patient avoids loading the heel
Footwear: wear pattern, cushioning, heel-to-toe drop and stiffness
Calf bulk, heel-pad swelling or bruising, and any visible plantar swelling or mass
palpation: Medial calcaneal tubercle and the proximal medial band of the plantar fascia: the usual site of tenderness
Compare with the heel pad centre (fat pad), lateral and medial calcaneal squeeze (stress fracture), the medial heel nerve path (Baxter's nerve) and the Achilles insertion
Plantar fascia mid-band for nodules or a defect (plantar fibroma, partial rupture)
rangeOfMotion: Ankle dorsiflexion with the knee straight and bent (gastrocnemius and soleus length); reduced dorsiflexion showed some association with heel pain [r9]
First MTP extension, non-weight-bearing and weight-bearing; reduced extension showed some association [r9]
Subtalar motion and foot posture index, for context only, because posture was not consistently linked to heel pain [r9]
strength: Single-leg heel raise capacity (repetitions and pain); higher plantar-flexor strength predicted improvement in a prognostic review [r12]
Toe plantar-flexion and intrinsic foot strength (paper grip or short-foot test); strength was lower in some people with heel pain, with very low certainty [r10]
Hip abductor and extensor strength as part of the kinetic chain
neuro: Sensation over the plantar foot and medial heel; Tinel's test over the tarsal tunnel and Baxter's nerve
Slump test and lumbosacral screen (S1) if pain is radiating or the foot examination is unremarkable
Vascular check (pulses, capillary refill) in older adults or people with diabetes
functional: Weight-bearing windlass test, heel walk and toe walk
Single-leg heel raise: repetitions to fatigue and pain response
Single-leg stance and single-leg squat for lower-limb control
Hop or running assessment in athletes (pain, landing mechanics and next-day response)

specialTests.name: Windlass test (weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing)
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce heel pain by tightening the plantar fascia with great-toe extension
specialTests.procedure: Non-weight-bearing: fully extend the first MTP joint with the ankle stabilised. Weight-bearing: extend the first MTP joint with the foot loaded, as described in the original study.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of the familiar plantar-medial heel pain
specialTests.sensitivity: 31.8% weight-bearing; 13.6% non-weight-bearing (7 and 3 of 22 patients with plantar fasciitis)
specialTests.specificity: 100% in that sample (none of 23 patients with other foot pain or 30 controls had pain)

specialTests.name: Palpation of the medial calcaneal tubercle
specialTests.purpose: Localise pain to the fascial origin
specialTests.procedure: With the ankle dorsiflexed and toes extended to tension the fascia, press firmly over the medial calcaneal tubercle and along the proximal medial band.
specialTests.positive: Focal tenderness that reproduces the familiar pain. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Single-leg heel raise
specialTests.purpose: Assess calf-foot capacity and provoke loaded pain; baseline for strength progression
specialTests.procedure: Stand on one leg and rise onto the toes repeatedly to fatigue or to a set limit. Record repetitions, range and pain.
specialTests.positive: Early fatigue, restricted height or reproduction of heel pain. No diagnostic accuracy figures were identified.

specialTests.name: Calcaneal squeeze test
specialTests.procedure: Squeeze the heel from medial and lateral sides with both hands.
specialTests.positive: Pain on compression of the calcaneal body suggests stress fracture or bone stress and needs imaging. No accuracy figures were identified.

specialTests.name: Tinel's test over the tarsal tunnel and Baxter's nerve
specialTests.procedure: Tap over the posterior tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus and along its plantar branches near the medial heel.
specialTests.positive: Tingling or burning radiating along the nerve distribution. No accuracy figures were identified.

clinicalRules.name: No validated diagnostic or prediction rule identified
clinicalRules.description: Diagnosis is clinical: gradual plantar-medial heel pain with first-step pain and focal tenderness. A prognostic review found that sex, bilateral symptoms, heel spur, ankle plantar-flexor strength and response to taping were associated with outcome, but study quality was low and no rule has been validated [r12].

outcomeMeasures.name: Foot Function Index (FFI)
outcomeMeasures.use: Self-reported foot pain, disability and activity limitation. It was the primary outcome in the high-load strength training RCT [r7].

outcomeMeasures.name: Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) or Foot Health Status Questionnaire
outcomeMeasures.use: Region-specific function and sport subscales for tracking change

outcomeMeasures.name: Numeric pain rating scale (0–10) for first-step pain and activity pain
outcomeMeasures.use: Simple tracking of the two key symptoms; record first-step pain and worst pain in the last week separately

outcomeMeasures.name: Single-leg heel raise repetitions
outcomeMeasures.use: Capacity measure to guide strength progression

imaging.indication: Not routine. Use for trauma, suspected stress fracture, bone lesion or when the diagnosis is uncertain.
imaging.findings: May show a calcaneal spur, which is associated with chronic heel pain [r9] but did not predict outcome [r1]. A spur does not confirm the pain source.

imaging.indication: When the diagnosis is unclear, to exclude a mass or partial tear, or to guide an injection
imaging.findings: Thickened, hypoechoic proximal fascia (about 6.7–6.9 mm at baseline in one cohort). Thickness fell over time whether or not symptoms persisted and did not predict prognosis [r1].

imaging.indication: When bone stress injury, a tumour, partial rupture or another cause is suspected, or when the diagnosis is still unclear after treatment
imaging.findings: Fascial thickening and signal change with possible calcaneal marrow oedema; also excludes stress fracture and neural causes

differentials.name: Heel fat pad syndrome or contusion
differentials.distinguishing: Central heel pain directly under the weight-bearing pad, worst on hard surfaces, with a history of impact. Tenderness is central rather than at the medial tubercle.

differentials.name: Calcaneal stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Pain increases through activity and persists at rest or night; positive medial–lateral calcaneal squeeze; usually after a sharp rise in load. Image to confirm.

differentials.name: Baxter's nerve entrapment or tarsal tunnel syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Burning, radiating or paraesthetic pain, worse at the end of the day, with a positive Tinel's test. It can coexist with fasciopathy.

differentials.name: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Posterior heel pain at the Achilles insertion, worse with dorsiflexion and uphill loading, not at the plantar-medial tubercle.

differentials.name: Calcaneal apophysitis (Sever's disease)
differentials.distinguishing: Activity-related heel pain in skeletally immature children, usually 8–14 years, with posterior heel tenderness and a positive squeeze test.

differentials.name: Plantar fascia rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden sharp pain with a pop, often after an injection or a push-off, with bruising, swelling and a palpable defect or arch loss.

differentials.name: Enthesitis in inflammatory arthropathy
differentials.distinguishing: Bilateral heel pain with prolonged morning stiffness, other enthesis or joint involvement, psoriasis, uveitis or bowel symptoms; refer for rheumatology review.

differentials.name: Plantar fibromatosis (Ledderhose disease)
differentials.distinguishing: A palpable, firm nodule in the mid-plantar fascia, not at the heel origin.

differentials.name: S1 radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Referred heel or sole pain with back or buttock symptoms, a positive slump or straight-leg raise and possible reflex or sensory change.

redFlags: Night pain, constant rest pain, unexplained weight loss, fever or a history of cancer: suspect infection, tumour or a stress fracture. Arrange urgent imaging and medical review.
Sudden severe pain with a pop, bruising or loss of the arch (especially after a corticosteroid injection): suspect plantar fascia rupture. Protect the foot and arrange review.
Pain that increases through activity and persists at rest after a rise in load, with a positive calcaneal squeeze test: suspect calcaneal stress fracture and image before loading.
Bilateral heel pain with morning stiffness longer than 30 minutes, other joint swelling, back pain, psoriasis, uveitis or bowel symptoms: refer for inflammatory arthropathy assessment [r1,r12].
Numbness, burning, weakness or radiating pain: examine for tarsal tunnel, Baxter's nerve or S1 involvement and refer if neurological signs are present.
Diabetes, peripheral neuropathy or poor circulation with heel pain or skin breakdown: urgent medical or podiatry review before starting loading, because of ulcer and infection risk.

management.principles: Treat plantar heel pain as a load-capacity problem. Educate the patient, adjust (rather than stop) load, and build capacity with progressive strengthening of the calf and foot, adding short-term symptom relief (taping, orthoses or footwear change) so that loading can continue [r7,r13]. A network meta-analysis of 31 RCTs found no evidence that any commonly used treatment was better than another; corticosteroid injection and shockwave ranked most likely to help, exercise appeared helpful only for long-term outcomes, and the data were sparse with wide confidence intervals [r6]. Clinical practice guidelines for physiotherapists exist for this condition [r2,r3]; only their abstracts could be read in the sources used for this page, so the recommendation grades are not reproduced here. Use shared decision-making, set a realistic timeline (months, not weeks) and reserve injection or surgery for the minority who do not improve with well-delivered loading [r1].

medical.name: Simple analgesia and short courses of NSAIDs
medical.description: Used for short-term pain control to allow loading. NSAIDs were included in a network meta-analysis that could not rank any treatment above another, and histology from chronic disease shows little inflammation [r6,r4].

medical.name: Single corticosteroid injection (ideally ultrasound-guided)
medical.description: In a meta-analysis of 47 trials, injection beat some comparators for short-term pain (autologous blood injection, foot orthoses) but was no better than placebo injection, and when high-risk-of-bias trials were removed there were no significant findings. In the longer term it was less effective than dry needling and platelet-rich plasma [r15]. In one cohort a US-guided injection did not cause fat-pad atrophy [r1].

medical.name: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection
medical.description: A meta-analysis of 10 RCTs (445 patients, mostly versus steroid) found PRP as effective as other treatments, with benefit over comparators at 12 months but not at 1, 3 or 6 months. Study numbers are small and the risk of bias is variable [r16,r15].

medical.name: Repeated or serial corticosteroid injections
medical.description: Not supported by the trial evidence, and histology showing degeneration without inflammation led to concern about plantar fascial rupture [r4,r15].

medical.name: Surgery (plantar fascia release or gastrocnemius recession)
medical.description: Reserved for long-standing pain that has not responded to many months of well-delivered non-operative care. Risks include arch change and nerve injury. No trial evidence was reviewed for this page.

physio.name: Education and load management
physio.description: Explain the load-capacity model and the expected timeline. Reduce or substitute high-load activity (long runs, prolonged standing, barefoot walking on hard floors), keep cross-training and rebuild gradually. Avoid complete rest.

physio.name: High-load strength training (heel raises)
physio.description: Progressive unilateral heel raises with a towel under the toes, every second day, plus shoe inserts. In 48 patients with ultrasound-confirmed plantar fasciitis the Foot Function Index was 29 points lower (95% CI 6–52) at 3 months than with inserts plus plantar-specific stretching; there were no differences at 1, 6 or 12 months [r7]. In the network meta-analysis exercise appeared beneficial only for long-term outcomes [r6].

physio.name: Plantar-fascia-specific stretching and calf stretching
physio.description: In a trial of 82 patients with chronic disease, a tissue-specific plantar fascia stretch beat Achilles stretching at 8 weeks, and by 2 years there was no group difference and 92% of 66 respondents were satisfied with treatment [r17]. In the strength RCT the stretch group had an FFI of 16 points at 12 months [r7]. A cheap, low-risk option that can run alongside strengthening.

physio.name: Foot orthoses and insoles
physio.description: A meta-analysis of 19 trials found moderate-quality evidence that orthoses reduce pain more than sham orthoses in the medium term (SMD −0.27, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.06; clinical importance uncertain), and very-low-quality evidence of no benefit in the short and longer term. Customised and prefabricated orthoses did not differ [r18]. Contoured full-length insoles were more effective than heel cups [r13].

physio.name: Rigid or low-Dye style taping
physio.description: A review of 43 articles found taping an effective short-term treatment [r13]. Response to taping was one of the strongest predictors of medium-term improvement in a small prognostic review, which suggests a trial of taping can guide orthosis choice [r12].

physio.name: Night splint, with insoles or rocker shoes
physio.description: Combining night splints or rocker shoes with insoles enhanced pain relief and function compared with any one of them alone, in a review with variable study quality [r13].

physio.name: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT)
physio.description: A meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found ESWT reduced pain (VAS change −2.8 focal and −3.0 radial), although outcomes and dropout depended on parameters (frequency, pulses, energy flux density) and the authors called for high-quality studies [r19]. ESWT ranked among the treatments most likely to help in the network meta-analysis, but no treatment was clearly better [r6]. Consider after a period of well-delivered loading has not helped.

physio.name: Manual therapy and soft-tissue release (calf, foot)
physio.description: Used as an adjunct to relieve pain and improve ankle and first MTP motion so loading is possible. No trial evidence was reviewed for this page.

physio.name: Footwear change and weight management
physio.description: Cushioned, supportive footwear and a gradual weight-management plan where BMI is high. Higher BMI and body mass were associated with plantar fasciitis in active people, but there is no trial showing that weight change alters outcome [r8].

physio.name: Address psychosocial factors
physio.description: Screen for fear of loading and catastrophising and address them with education and graded exposure. Both were associated with worse foot function and first-step pain, although the evidence is cross-sectional [r11].

physio.name: Complete rest or prolonged unloading
physio.description: Unloading does not build capacity and leaves the fascia less able to tolerate return to activity. Modify load instead.

education: The fascia is not torn. The tissue has been overloaded and has become thick and sensitive, and its capacity can be rebuilt with progressive loading.
First-step pain is typical and does not mean you are making it worse. Pain that stays higher the next day after exercise means the load was too much.
Expect improvement over months. Many people are still symptomatic at 12 months, but most do eventually settle [r1].
Heel raises and stretching both work. In one trial strength training helped faster, and by 6 months the results were the same.
A heel spur is not the cause of the pain, and scans do not need to look normal for your pain to settle [r1].
Taping, inserts and shockwave can help ease symptoms but do not replace the strengthening program.
Injections can give short-term relief but are not clearly better than placebo, and repeated injections are not advised [r15].

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and follows the load-capacity model: settle the foot with education, taping or inserts and load control; then build strength with high-load heel raises; then restore impact capacity; then return to running and sport. Move on when the objective criteria are met, not when a set number of weeks has passed. Stage timeframes are typical, and a long-standing foot will take longer. Dosages are typical clinical ranges based on the trial protocols cited and on clinical practice, not prescriptions from a single source: the strength RCT abstract specifies unilateral heel raises with a towel under the toes performed every second day, with the load progressed over the trial [r7]. As a working rule, pain during exercise should stay at or below about 4/10 and settle within 24 hours (clinical convention).

stages.name: Settle & educate
goals: Reduce first-step pain and loaded pain
Remove load spikes while keeping the patient active
Start gentle calf and foot loading
Educate on the load-capacity model and timeline
precautions: Do not rest completely; modify load instead
Keep exercise pain at or below about 4/10 and settled within 24 hours (clinical convention)
Screen red flags (stress fracture, nerve, inflammatory) before loading

exercises.name: Plantar-fascia-specific stretch (toes pulled back, seated, ankle crossed over knee)
exercises.dosage: 10 reps × 10 s hold, 3 times daily, including before the first steps in the morning (clinical convention based on the stretching trials)
exercises.cues: Pull the toes back until you feel a stretch in the arch, and check that the arch is firm along the fascia

exercises.name: Calf stretch against a wall (knee straight, then bent)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 30 s each position, twice daily
exercises.cues: Keep the heel down and the foot straight

exercises.name: Seated calf raise (soleus)
exercises.dosage: 2 × 15, slow, daily
exercises.cues: Press through the ball of the foot, pause at the top

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise (flat floor)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 12–15, 3 s up and 3 s down, daily
exercises.cues: Weight evenly over both feet

exercises.name: Short-foot and toe-curl (towel scrunch)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10, daily
exercises.cues: Draw the ball of the foot toward the heel without curling the toes

exercises.name: Low-impact conditioning (cycling or pool)
exercises.dosage: 20–30 min, 3 times a week, below the pain threshold
exercises.cues: Maintain fitness without heavy heel loading

progressionCriteria: First-step pain at or below 4/10 and not worsening week to week
Double-leg calf raise × 15 with pain at or below 3/10
Walks 20–30 min with pain at or below 3/10 and settled within 24 h

stages.name: High-load strength
goals: Build calf and foot strength and tolerance of tensile load
Restore normal walking, stair and standing tolerance
Reduce first-step pain and improve the Foot Function Index
Continue taping or inserts if they help
precautions: Progress load only if the previous session has settled within 24 h
Pain during sets should stay at or below about 4/10
Heel raises every second day: allow recovery between loaded sessions [r7]

exercises.name: Single-leg heel raise with a rolled towel under the toes (the trial exercise)
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 8–12 slow reps (3 s up, 2 s hold, 3 s down), every second day; progress load by adding a backpack as pain allows (clinical convention based on the trial protocol) [r7]
exercises.cues: Toes stay extended over the towel so the fascia is loaded in the windlass position

exercises.name: Seated calf raise with load (soleus)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–15 with a dumbbell on the knee, 3 times a week
exercises.cues: Slow lowering, full range

exercises.name: Split squat (heel down)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–10 each leg, 3 times a week
exercises.cues: Front knee over the second toe, weight through the whole foot

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–10, twice a week
exercises.cues: Hinge at the hips with a long spine; posterior chain support for the foot

exercises.name: Single-leg balance (foot short and arch active)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 30–45 s each side, daily
exercises.cues: Soft knee, quiet trunk, keep the arch lifted

progressionCriteria: Single-leg heel raise × 15 with pain at or below 3/10 and no next-day flare (clinical convention)
First-step pain at or below 3/10 and improving
Foot Function Index clearly improved from baseline

stages.name: Capacity & impact
goals: Raise strength toward heavy single-leg loads
precautions: Add impact volume gradually and leave at least 48 h between impact sessions
Stop progressing if pain is higher the next morning
Keep heavy calf strengthening going alongside impact

exercises.name: Heavy single-leg calf raise (loaded)
exercises.dosage: 3–4 × 6–10 with added weight, 2–3 times a week
exercises.cues: Slow tempo; full range; toes extended

exercises.name: Step-up with heel drive
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–10 each leg
exercises.cues: Control the pelvis and push through the whole foot

exercises.name: Skipping rope or bilateral low hops
exercises.dosage: 3 × 20–30 s, twice a week, at pain at or below 3/10
exercises.cues: Quiet landings on the forefoot

exercises.name: Single-leg hop progressions (in place, then forward)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 5–10 each leg, twice a week
exercises.cues: Soft landing, stick for 2 s

exercises.name: Brisk walking intervals or incline walking
exercises.dosage: 20–30 min, 3 times a week
exercises.cues: Push off through the great toe

progressionCriteria: Heavy single-leg calf raise × 6–10 with pain at or below 3/10 and no next-day flare
Low-level hopping with pain at or below 2/10 and a quiet next day
Tolerates 30–40 min of brisk walking pain-free

stages.name: Return to running & sport
goals: Return to running with a graded walk–run program
Hold the load-capacity balance as volume rises
precautions: Increase running volume stepwise and check next-morning first-step pain
Do not progress during a flare; step back one stage

exercises.name: Walk–run program
exercises.dosage: Start with 1 min run / 2 min walk for 20 min, 3 times a week, and add 1 min of running every 1–2 sessions if the next morning is settled (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Short, quick steps and a soft landing

exercises.name: Continuous running with surface and volume progression
exercises.dosage: Increase weekly volume by about 10% (clinical convention); easy surfaces first
exercises.cues: Monitor first-step pain the next morning

exercises.name: Planned then reactive change of direction
exercises.dosage: 2 sessions a week, increasing speed and angle
exercises.cues: Land under control, with the knee over the foot

exercises.name: Heavy calf and foot strength maintenance
exercises.dosage: 2 times a week, 3–4 × 6–8, all year
exercises.cues: Keep the tempo slow and the load heavy

progressionCriteria: Runs 30 min continuously with pain at or below 2/10 and no next-morning increase
Single-leg heel raise × 20 or more with equal height on both sides
Completes full training for 2 weeks without a flare
Foot Function Index near the patient's goal

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified for plantar heel pain; the criteria below reflect clinical convention
First-step pain at or below 2/10 and no next-morning flare after a loaded session
Single-leg heel raise × 20 or more with symmetrical height, and heavy loaded calf work tolerated
Walk–run program completed to continuous running at the target volume without a symptom flare
Hop and landing tasks pain-free and symmetrical, with agreed sport-specific tasks tolerated
A maintenance strength and load-monitoring plan is in place
tests: Single-leg heel raise repetitions and range
Foot Function Index or FAAM sport subscale
Single-leg hop tests with pain rating
Weekly running volume log with next-morning first-step pain

prognosis: Plantar heel pain is not reliably self-limiting. In a hospital cohort of 174 patients followed for a mean of 9.7 years, 54% were asymptomatic at follow-up, and the risk of still having plantar fasciitis was 80.5% at 1 year, 50.0% at 5 years and 44.0% at 15 years. Women and those with bilateral pain did worse [r1]. This cohort attended a diagnostic centre and received varied treatment, so it may overstate persistence in the wider population. A small prognostic review found that sex and bilateral symptoms predicted poorer outcome in one cohort, while heel spur, ankle plantar-flexor strength and response to taping predicted medium-term improvement; study quality was low and psychosocial factors were not studied [r12]. In the high-load strength RCT the Foot Function Index at 12 months was 22 points (strength) and 16 points (stretch) [r7]. In a 2-year follow-up of a stretching trial, 94% of 66 respondents reported less pain [r17].
prevention: Build running, standing and walking volume gradually and avoid sudden increases or hard surface and footwear changes (clinical observation; no prevention trial identified).
Maintain calf and foot strength throughout the year, since muscle weakness is associated with heel pain (very low certainty) [r10].
Address modifiable load factors such as high body mass in active people [r8].
Act early on first-step pain with load modification and strengthening rather than waiting for it to become persistent [r1].
Replace worn running shoes and match cushioning and stiffness to the activity (clinical convention).
clinicalPearls: First-step pain is the hallmark, but a plantar fasciopathy that has become loaded and chronic can hurt through the day. Pair the history with focal medial calcaneal tubercle tenderness.

A negative windlass test does not rule out plantar fasciopathy: sensitivity was 31.8% weight-bearing and 13.6% non-weight-bearing in the original study, though specificity was 100% in that small sample [r14].
Do not chase the scan. Fascia thickness fell in both asymptomatic and symptomatic patients and heel spur did not predict outcome, so imaging should not drive load or injection decisions [r1].
Strength training beat stretching at 3 months but not at 6 or 12 months, so choose by tolerance and adherence and give a realistic timeline [r7].
Injection gives, at most, short-term relief and was not better than placebo injection. Avoid repeated injections, given the histological concern about fascial rupture [r15,r4].
Bilateral heel pain, female sex and a poor response to initial care predict a longer course. Screen for an inflammatory cause and set expectations early [r1,r12].

forces.label: Load repeats at the heel origin

captions.text: A runner lands heel-first. The heel fat pad cushions each step.
As the arch lowers, the plantar fascia lengthens and takes tensile load.
At push-off the toes extend and the windlass tightens the fascia to stiffen the foot.
That load passes into the fascia's origin on the heel bone, step after step.
If load rises faster than the fascia can adapt, its origin begins to change.
There is no single injury: the heel becomes painful with the first steps after rest.
Zooming into the right foot, viewed from the inner (medial) side.
The plantar fascia runs from the medial calcaneal tubercle to the forefoot and supports the arch.
The ground pushes up while toe extension winds the fascia tight, so it carries tension.
Peak tension is concentrated at the fascia's attachment on the heel bone.
With repeated overload the fascia at its origin thickens.
Pain is focused at the medial heel and is worst with the first steps after rest.
The tissue degenerates, with disorganised collagen, rather than inflaming. It does not tear.
A nearby nerve and the heel pad can add to or mimic the pain, so examine for them.
Healthy fascia: dense, aligned type I collagen running along the line of tension.
Overload: repeated tension causes microscopic collagen damage at the heel origin.
Degeneration: the matrix breaks down and the collagen becomes disorganised, with little inflammation.
The fascia thickens at its origin, and the tissue stays sensitive.
Progressive loading rebuilds capacity. Symptoms settle before the structure fully normalises.
